<script type="application/json" id="pack-y1w18">{"year":1,"week":18,"id":"y1w18","title":"Trigonometric Ratios, Special Angles and Angles up to 360°","subtitle":"Opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse; sine, cosine and tangent; exact values for 30°, 45° and 60°; angles in all four quadrants; heights and distances using angles of elevation and depression.","family":"geometry","section":{"no":3,"name":"Geometry and Measurement","strand":"Geometry Around Us","from":13,"to":20},"outcomes":["Name the opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse sides for a given angle.","Use sine, cosine and tangent to find sides and angles in right-angled triangles.","Derive and use the exact ratios of $30^\\circ$, $45^\\circ$ and $60^\\circ$.","Find the sign and value of trigonometric ratios for angles from $0^\\circ$ to $360^\\circ$.","Solve problems on heights and distances using angles of elevation and depression."],"keywords":["opposite","adjacent","hypotenuse","sine","cosine","tangent","SOHCAHTOA","exact values","unit circle","quadrant","reference angle","angle of elevation","angle of depression"],"notes":[{"title":"Naming the sides","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Trigonometry links the **angles** of a triangle to the **lengths** of its sides. It lets us find heights and distances that are hard or dangerous to measure directly."},{"k":"p","text":"In a right-angled triangle, choose one of the acute angles and call it $\\theta$ (theta). Then:"},{"k":"ul","items":["the **hypotenuse** is the longest side, opposite the right angle;","the **opposite** side is the side facing $\\theta$;","the **adjacent** side is the side next to $\\theta$ that is not the hypotenuse."]},{"k":"fig","id":"w18-sides","caption":"The names opposite and adjacent depend on which angle you choose; the hypotenuse never changes."}],"figs":["w18-sides"]},{"title":"Sine, cosine and tangent","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"The trigonometric ratios","blocks":[{"k":"math","tex":"\\sin\\theta=\\frac{\\text{opposite}}{\\text{hypotenuse}}\\qquad\\cos\\theta=\\frac{\\text{adjacent}}{\\text{hypotenuse}}\\qquad\\tan\\theta=\\frac{\\text{opposite}}{\\text{adjacent}}"}]},{"k":"box","kind":"tip","title":"Remember SOH–CAH–TOA","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"**S**ine $=$ **O**pposite $\\div$ **H**ypotenuse; **C**osine $=$ **A**djacent $\\div$ **H**ypotenuse; **T**angent $=$ **O**pposite $\\div$ **A**djacent. Label the sides on the diagram first, then choose the ratio that links the side you know to the side you want."}]},{"k":"ul","items":["**To find a side:** write the ratio, then rearrange. For example, $\\tan40^\\circ=\\dfrac{x}{16}$ gives $x=16\\tan40^\\circ$.","**To find an angle:** use the inverse function. For example, if $\\sin\\theta=0.28$, then $\\theta=\\sin^{-1}0.28\\approx16.3^\\circ$."]},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Calculator in degrees","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Set your calculator to **DEG** mode. In RAD mode the answers are completely different."}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Exact values for $30^\\circ$, $45^\\circ$ and $60^\\circ$","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Cut an equilateral triangle of side 2 in half: you get a triangle with sides $1$, $\\sqrt{3}$ and $2$ and angles $30^\\circ$, $60^\\circ$ and $90^\\circ$. Cut a square of side 1 along a diagonal: you get a triangle with sides $1$, $1$ and $\\sqrt{2}$ and angles $45^\\circ$, $45^\\circ$ and $90^\\circ$."},{"k":"fig","id":"w18-special","caption":"These two triangles give the exact ratios for $30^\\circ$, $45^\\circ$ and $60^\\circ$."},{"k":"table","head":["","$0^\\circ$","$30^\\circ$","$45^\\circ$","$60^\\circ$","$90^\\circ$"],"rows":[["$\\sin$","$0$","$\\dfrac{1}{2}$","$\\dfrac{\\sqrt{2}}{2}$","$\\dfrac{\\sqrt{3}}{2}$","$1$"],["$\\cos$","$1$","$\\dfrac{\\sqrt{3}}{2}$","$\\dfrac{\\sqrt{2}}{2}$","$\\dfrac{1}{2}$","$0$"],["$\\tan$","$0$","$\\dfrac{1}{\\sqrt{3}}$","$1$","$\\sqrt{3}$","undefined"]]},{"k":"p","text":"Note that $\\dfrac{1}{\\sqrt{3}}=\\dfrac{\\sqrt{3}}{3}$ and $\\dfrac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}=\\dfrac{\\sqrt{2}}{2}$."}],"figs":["w18-special"]},{"title":"Angles from $0^\\circ$ to $360^\\circ$","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Place the angle with its vertex at the origin, starting from the positive $x$-axis and turning **anticlockwise**. Its end arm can lie in any of the four quadrants. On a circle of radius 1 (the **unit circle**), the point on the end arm has coordinates $(\\cos\\theta,\\ \\sin\\theta)$."},{"k":"fig","id":"w18-unitcircle","caption":"On the unit circle $x=\\cos\\theta$ and $y=\\sin\\theta$. The signs of $x$ and $y$ in each quadrant decide which ratios are positive."},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Which ratios are positive? (ASTC)","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["Quadrant I ($0^\\circ$–$90^\\circ$): **A**ll are positive.","Quadrant II ($90^\\circ$–$180^\\circ$): only **S**ine is positive.","Quadrant III ($180^\\circ$–$270^\\circ$): only **T**angent is positive.","Quadrant IV ($270^\\circ$–$360^\\circ$): only **C**osine is positive."]}]},{"k":"p","text":"The **reference angle** is the acute angle between the end arm and the $x$-axis. Find the value for the reference angle, then attach the sign for the quadrant."},{"k":"fig","id":"w18-reference","caption":"The reference angle is measured to the nearest part of the $x$-axis."},{"k":"table","head":["Quadrant","Reference angle for $\\theta$","Example"],"rows":[["II","$180^\\circ-\\theta$","$\\sin150^\\circ=+\\sin30^\\circ=\\dfrac{1}{2}$"],["III","$\\theta-180^\\circ$","$\\cos210^\\circ=-\\cos30^\\circ=-\\dfrac{\\sqrt{3}}{2}$"],["IV","$360^\\circ-\\theta$","$\\tan315^\\circ=-\\tan45^\\circ=-1$"]]},{"k":"p","text":"**On the axes:** $\\sin0^\\circ=0$, $\\cos0^\\circ=1$; $\\sin90^\\circ=1$, $\\cos90^\\circ=0$; $\\sin180^\\circ=0$, $\\cos180^\\circ=-1$; $\\sin270^\\circ=-1$, $\\cos270^\\circ=0$. Since $\\tan\\theta=\\dfrac{\\sin\\theta}{\\cos\\theta}$, the tangent is **undefined** at $90^\\circ$ and $270^\\circ$, where the cosine is $0$."},{"k":"fig","id":"w18-graphs","caption":"The graphs of $\\sin x$ and $\\cos x$ repeat every $360^\\circ$ and stay between $-1$ and $1$."}],"figs":["w18-unitcircle","w18-reference","w18-graphs"]},{"title":"Angles of elevation and depression","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The **angle of elevation** is measured **up** from the horizontal to the line of sight. The **angle of depression** is measured **down** from the horizontal. Both are measured from the horizontal, never from the vertical."},{"k":"fig","id":"w18-elevation","caption":"Elevation: looking up from the horizontal. Depression: looking down from the horizontal."},{"k":"p","text":"For an object of height $h$ at a horizontal distance $d$, with angle of elevation $\\theta$: $\\tan\\theta=\\dfrac{h}{d}$, so $h=d\\tan\\theta$. If the angle is measured at eye level, **add** the height of the observer’s eye to get the full height."},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Common errors","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["$\\sin(a+b)\\neq\\sin a+\\sin b$.","$\\sin^{-1}x$ means the angle whose sine is $x$; it is **not** $\\dfrac{1}{\\sin x}$.","Round only at the end of a calculation."]}]}],"figs":["w18-elevation"]}],"examples":[{"title":"Ratios from two sides","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"In a right-angled triangle the side opposite the acute angle $\\theta$ is 9 cm and the adjacent side is 12 cm. Find $\\sin\\theta$, $\\cos\\theta$ and $\\tan\\theta$."}],"steps":["Hypotenuse: $h^2=9^2+12^2=225$, so $h=15$ cm.","$\\sin\\theta=\\dfrac{9}{15}=\\dfrac{3}{5}$.","$\\cos\\theta=\\dfrac{12}{15}=\\dfrac{4}{5}$ and $\\tan\\theta=\\dfrac{9}{12}=\\dfrac{3}{4}$."],"answer":"$\\sin\\theta=\\dfrac{3}{5}$, $\\cos\\theta=\\dfrac{4}{5}$, $\\tan\\theta=\\dfrac{3}{4}$","figs":[]},{"title":"A ladder at $60^\\circ$","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"An 8 m ladder makes an angle of $60^\\circ$ with level ground. How high up the wall does it reach? Give an exact answer and a 2 d.p. answer."}],"steps":["The ladder is the hypotenuse; the height is opposite the $60^\\circ$ angle.","$\\sin60^\\circ=\\dfrac{h}{8}$, so $h=8\\sin60^\\circ$.","$h=8\\times\\dfrac{\\sqrt{3}}{2}=4\\sqrt{3}\\approx6.93$."],"answer":"$4\\sqrt{3}$ m $\\approx6.93$ m","figs":[]},{"title":"The height of a building","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A learner stands 24 m from a building. The angle of elevation of the roof, measured from her eye level of 1.6 m, is $35^\\circ$. Find the height of the building to 2 d.p."}],"steps":["Height above eye level: $\\tan35^\\circ=\\dfrac{h}{24}$, so $h=24\\tan35^\\circ=16.80498\\ldots$","Add the eye height: $H=16.80498\\ldots+1.6=18.40498\\ldots$","Round only now: $H\\approx18.40$ m."],"answer":"About 18.40 m","figs":[]},{"title":"Exact values beyond $90^\\circ$","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Find the exact values of $\\sin150^\\circ$, $\\cos210^\\circ$ and $\\tan315^\\circ$, explaining each sign."}],"steps":["$150^\\circ$ is in quadrant II (reference angle $30^\\circ$), where sine is positive: $\\sin150^\\circ=\\sin30^\\circ=\\dfrac{1}{2}$.","$210^\\circ$ is in quadrant III (reference angle $30^\\circ$), where cosine is negative: $\\cos210^\\circ=-\\cos30^\\circ=-\\dfrac{\\sqrt{3}}{2}$.","$315^\\circ$ is in quadrant IV (reference angle $45^\\circ$), where tangent is negative: $\\tan315^\\circ=-\\tan45^\\circ=-1$."],"answer":"$\\dfrac{1}{2}$, $\\;-\\dfrac{\\sqrt{3}}{2}$, $\\;-1$","figs":[]},{"title":"Finding a side with tangent","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A right-angled triangle has an angle of $40^\\circ$, and the side adjacent to it is 16 cm. Find the opposite side to 2 d.p."}],"steps":["Opposite and adjacent are linked by tangent: $\\tan40^\\circ=\\dfrac{x}{16}$.","$x=16\\tan40^\\circ=13.4256\\ldots$"],"answer":"About 13.43 cm","figs":[]},{"title":"A $30^\\circ$–$60^\\circ$–$90^\\circ$ triangle","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A $30^\\circ$–$60^\\circ$–$90^\\circ$ triangle has a hypotenuse of 18 cm. Find the two other sides exactly."}],"steps":["The shortest side is opposite $30^\\circ$: $\\sin30^\\circ=\\dfrac{a}{18}=\\dfrac{1}{2}$, so $a=9$ cm.","The other side is opposite $60^\\circ$: $\\sin60^\\circ=\\dfrac{b}{18}=\\dfrac{\\sqrt{3}}{2}$, so $b=9\\sqrt{3}$ cm.","Check: $9^2+(9\\sqrt{3})^2=81+243=324=18^2$ ✓."],"answer":"9 cm and $9\\sqrt{3}$ cm","figs":[]},{"title":"A tree’s shadow","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A tree casts a shadow 14 m long when the angle of elevation of the sun is $52^\\circ$. Find the height of the tree to 1 d.p."}],"steps":["Assume level ground and a vertical tree. The height is opposite the angle; the shadow is adjacent.","$\\tan52^\\circ=\\dfrac{h}{14}$, so $h=14\\tan52^\\circ=17.919\\ldots$"],"answer":"About 17.9 m","figs":[]},{"title":"Solving $\\sin\\theta=\\tfrac{1}{2}$","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Find all angles $\\theta$ with $\\sin\\theta=\\dfrac{1}{2}$ for $0^\\circ\\leq\\theta<360^\\circ$."}],"steps":["The acute angle with sine $\\dfrac{1}{2}$ is $30^\\circ$.","Sine is positive in quadrants I and II.","Quadrant I: $\\theta=30^\\circ$. Quadrant II: $\\theta=180^\\circ-30^\\circ=150^\\circ$."],"answer":"$\\theta=30^\\circ$ or $150^\\circ$","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Key results for Week 18","items":["$\\sin\\theta=\\dfrac{\\text{opp}}{\\text{hyp}}$, $\\;\\cos\\theta=\\dfrac{\\text{adj}}{\\text{hyp}}$, $\\;\\tan\\theta=\\dfrac{\\text{opp}}{\\text{adj}}$","$\\sin30^\\circ=\\cos60^\\circ=\\dfrac{1}{2}$; $\\;\\sin45^\\circ=\\cos45^\\circ=\\dfrac{\\sqrt{2}}{2}$; $\\;\\sin60^\\circ=\\cos30^\\circ=\\dfrac{\\sqrt{3}}{2}$","$\\tan30^\\circ=\\dfrac{1}{\\sqrt{3}}$, $\\;\\tan45^\\circ=1$, $\\;\\tan60^\\circ=\\sqrt{3}$","ASTC: All (I), Sin (II), Tan (III), Cos (IV) are positive.","Height from elevation: $h=d\\tan\\theta$ (add eye height if needed)."]}],"quiz":[{"q":"Which ratio equals $\\dfrac{\\text{opposite}}{\\text{hypotenuse}}$?","options":["cosine","sine","tangent","none of these"],"correct":1,"explain":"SOH: sine $=$ opposite $\\div$ hypotenuse."},{"q":"What is $\\sin30^\\circ$?","options":["$\\dfrac{\\sqrt{3}}{2}$","$1$","$\\dfrac{1}{2}$","$0$"],"correct":2,"explain":"In the $30^\\circ$–$60^\\circ$–$90^\\circ$ triangle, $\\sin30^\\circ=\\dfrac{1}{2}$."},{"q":"Find $\\tan45^\\circ$.","options":["$1$","$0$","$\\sqrt{3}$","undefined"],"correct":0,"explain":"The two legs of a right-angled isosceles triangle are equal, so their ratio is 1."},{"q":"What is $\\cos180^\\circ$?","options":["$1$","$0$","undefined","$-1$"],"correct":3,"explain":"At $180^\\circ$ the point on the unit circle is $(-1,0)$."},{"q":"In which quadrant are both sine and cosine negative?","options":["I","III","II","IV"],"correct":1,"explain":"In quadrant III both coordinates are negative."},{"q":"Find $\\sin150^\\circ$.","options":["$-\\dfrac{1}{2}$","$-\\dfrac{\\sqrt{3}}{2}$","$\\dfrac{1}{2}$","$\\dfrac{\\sqrt{3}}{2}$"],"correct":2,"explain":"Reference angle $30^\\circ$; sine is positive in quadrant II."},{"q":"At which angle is the tangent undefined?","options":["$90^\\circ$","$180^\\circ$","$0^\\circ$","$360^\\circ$"],"correct":0,"explain":"$\\tan\\theta=\\dfrac{\\sin\\theta}{\\cos\\theta}$, and $\\cos90^\\circ=0$."},{"q":"A right-angled triangle has opposite side 6 cm and adjacent side 8 cm. Find $\\tan\\theta$.","options":["$\\dfrac{4}{3}$","$\\dfrac{3}{5}$","$\\dfrac{4}{5}$","$\\dfrac{3}{4}$"],"correct":3,"explain":"$\\tan\\theta=\\dfrac{6}{8}=\\dfrac{3}{4}$."},{"q":"Find $\\cos60^\\circ$.","options":["$0$","$\\dfrac{1}{2}$","$\\dfrac{\\sqrt{3}}{2}$","$1$"],"correct":1,"explain":"$\\cos60^\\circ=\\dfrac{1}{2}$."},{"q":"Solve $\\tan\\theta=1$ for an acute angle $\\theta$.","options":["$30^\\circ$","$60^\\circ$","$45^\\circ$","$90^\\circ$"],"correct":2,"explain":"Among acute angles, $\\tan\\theta=1$ only at $45^\\circ$."}],"exercise":[{"q":"In a right-angled triangle, the opposite side is 15 cm and the adjacent side is 20 cm. Find the three ratios exactly.","a":"Hypotenuse 25 cm: $\\sin\\theta=\\dfrac{3}{5}$, $\\cos\\theta=\\dfrac{4}{5}$, $\\tan\\theta=\\dfrac{3}{4}$."},{"q":"From a point 35 m from a building, the angle of elevation of the top is $28^\\circ$. Find the height (ignore eye level).","a":"$35\\tan28^\\circ\\approx18.61$ m"},{"q":"Find the exact values of $\\sin240^\\circ$, $\\cos300^\\circ$ and $\\tan135^\\circ$.","a":"$-\\dfrac{\\sqrt{3}}{2}$, $\\;\\dfrac{1}{2}$, $\\;-1$"},{"q":"Find all angles with $\\cos\\theta=\\dfrac{1}{2}$ for $0^\\circ\\leq\\theta<360^\\circ$.","a":"$60^\\circ$ and $300^\\circ$"},{"q":"A 12 m cable makes an angle of $48^\\circ$ with level ground. How high does it reach?","a":"$12\\sin48^\\circ\\approx8.92$ m"},{"q":"In a right-angled triangle the opposite side is 7 cm and the hypotenuse is 25 cm. Find the angle $\\theta$ to 1 d.p.","a":"$\\sin\\theta=\\dfrac{7}{25}=0.28$, so $\\theta\\approx16.3^\\circ$."},{"q":"From the top of a 50 m cliff, the angle of depression of a boat is $20^\\circ$. How far is the boat from the foot of the cliff?","a":"$\\tan20^\\circ=\\dfrac{50}{d}$, so $d=\\dfrac{50}{\\tan20^\\circ}\\approx137.4$ m."},{"q":"Without a calculator, find $\\tan60^\\circ\\times\\cos30^\\circ$.","a":"$\\sqrt{3}\\times\\dfrac{\\sqrt{3}}{2}=\\dfrac{3}{2}$"}],"theory":[{"q":"Explain how to decide which side is opposite, which is adjacent and which is the hypotenuse.","steps":["The hypotenuse is always the side opposite the right angle (the longest side).","The opposite side is the side facing the chosen angle $\\theta$.","The adjacent side is the remaining side, which touches $\\theta$.","If you choose the other acute angle, opposite and adjacent swap; the hypotenuse stays the same."],"answer":"Find the right angle first, then label the sides relative to the chosen angle.","model":null},{"q":"Derive the exact values of $\\sin45^\\circ$ and $\\cos45^\\circ$.","steps":["Take a square of side 1. Its diagonal is $\\sqrt{1^2+1^2}=\\sqrt{2}$.","Half of the square is a right-angled triangle with angles $45^\\circ$, $45^\\circ$ and $90^\\circ$ and sides $1$, $1$, $\\sqrt{2}$.","$\\sin45^\\circ=\\dfrac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}$ and $\\cos45^\\circ=\\dfrac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}$."],"answer":"$\\sin45^\\circ=\\cos45^\\circ=\\dfrac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}=\\dfrac{\\sqrt{2}}{2}$","model":null},{"q":"A flagpole stands 20 m from an observer at ground level. The angle of elevation of the top is $42^\\circ$. Find the height of the pole to 2 d.p.","steps":["$\\tan42^\\circ=\\dfrac{h}{20}$.","$h=20\\tan42^\\circ=18.008\\ldots$"],"answer":"About 18.01 m","model":null},{"q":"Find the exact values of $\\sin120^\\circ$, $\\cos225^\\circ$ and $\\tan330^\\circ$, explaining the signs.","steps":["$120^\\circ$: quadrant II, reference $60^\\circ$, sine positive: $\\sin120^\\circ=\\dfrac{\\sqrt{3}}{2}$.","$225^\\circ$: quadrant III, reference $45^\\circ$, cosine negative: $\\cos225^\\circ=-\\dfrac{\\sqrt{2}}{2}$.","$330^\\circ$: quadrant IV, reference $30^\\circ$, tangent negative: $\\tan330^\\circ=-\\dfrac{1}{\\sqrt{3}}$."],"answer":"$\\dfrac{\\sqrt{3}}{2}$, $\\;-\\dfrac{\\sqrt{2}}{2}$, $\\;-\\dfrac{1}{\\sqrt{3}}$","model":null},{"q":"Find the two angles between $0^\\circ$ and $360^\\circ$ for which $\\cos\\theta=-\\dfrac{1}{2}$.","steps":["The reference angle is $60^\\circ$, because $\\cos60^\\circ=\\dfrac{1}{2}$.","Cosine is negative in quadrants II and III.","Quadrant II: $180^\\circ-60^\\circ=120^\\circ$. <script type="application/json" id="pack-y1w19">{"year":1,"week":19,"id":"y1w19","title":"Measurement, Perimeter and Area of Plane Shapes","subtitle":"Referents and units; converting units of length and area; perimeter; areas of rectangles, triangles, parallelograms, trapeziums and circles; composite and irregular shapes; costing problems.","family":"geometry","section":{"no":3,"name":"Geometry and Measurement","strand":"Geometry Around Us","from":13,"to":20},"outcomes":["Use sensible referents to estimate lengths and areas, and convert between units of length and area.","Calculate the perimeter and area of common plane shapes, including circles.","Find the area of composite shapes by adding and subtracting parts, and estimate irregular areas on a grid.","Solve fencing, flooring, tiling and painting problems, including costs.","Explain how the area changes when lengths are scaled."],"keywords":["referent","unit conversion","perimeter","circumference","area","square unit","hectare","composite shape","annulus","estimate","scale factor"],"notes":[{"title":"What measurement means","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"To **measure** is to compare a quantity with an agreed unit. A **referent** is a familiar object used to estimate a size: a classroom door is about 1 m wide, and a square 1 m by 1 m has an area of 1 m². A referent gives an **estimate**; use a ruler or tape when you need accuracy."},{"k":"ul","items":["**Length** is a distance in one direction (m, cm, km).","**Perimeter** is the distance all the way round a shape (also a length).","**Area** is the amount of surface inside a boundary (m², cm², hectares)."]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Converting units","blocks":[{"k":"table","head":["Length","Area"],"rows":[["$1$ km $=1000$ m","$1$ km² $=1\\,000\\,000$ m²"],["$1$ m $=100$ cm","$1$ m² $=10\\,000$ cm²"],["$1$ cm $=10$ mm","$1$ cm² $=100$ mm²"],["$1$ inch $=2.54$ cm","$1$ hectare (ha) $=10\\,000$ m²"]]},{"k":"fig","id":"w19-units","caption":"A square metre is 100 cm by 100 cm, so it contains $100\\times100=10\\,000$ square centimetres."},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Square the conversion factor for area","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Since $1$ m $=100$ cm, $1$ m² $=100^2$ cm² $=10\\,000$ cm². This matters when you buy tiles or paint."}]}],"figs":["w19-units"]},{"title":"Perimeter","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The perimeter is the total length of the boundary, given in units of length (m, cm)."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Perimeters","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["Rectangle: $P=2(l+b)$","Square: $P=4a$","Triangle: $P=a+b+c$","Circle (circumference): $C=2\\pi r=\\pi d$"]}]},{"k":"p","text":"For a composite shape, walk round the **outside** only; do not add the lines inside the shape."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Areas of common shapes","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Area is given in **square units**. The dashed lines show the perpendicular heights."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Areas","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["Rectangle: $A=lb$; $\\;$ square: $A=a^2$","Triangle: $A=\\tfrac{1}{2}bh$","Parallelogram: $A=bh$","Trapezium: $A=\\tfrac{1}{2}(a+b)h$, where $a$ and $b$ are the parallel sides","Circle: $A=\\pi r^2$"]}]}],"figs":["w19-shapes"]},{"title":"Composite and irregular shapes","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A **composite** shape is made of simpler shapes. Mark all the lengths, split the shape with a dividing line, find each area, then **add** the parts. If a piece has been cut out, **subtract** its area."},{"k":"fig","id":"w19-lshape","caption":"The L-shape is a $16\\times12$ rectangle with a $6\\times5$ corner removed: $192-30=162$ m²."},{"k":"p","text":"An **annulus** (ring) is the region between two circles with the same centre: $A=\\pi R^2-\\pi r^2=\\pi(R^2-r^2)$."},{"k":"fig","id":"w19-annulus","caption":"The walkway is the outer circle minus the pond."},{"k":"p","text":"**Irregular shapes** drawn on squared paper can be estimated: count the whole squares, and count each part square as about half."},{"k":"fig","id":"w19-grid","caption":"Whole squares count 1; part squares count about $\\frac{1}{2}$ each. The answer is an estimate."}],"figs":["w19-lshape","w19-annulus","w19-grid"]},{"title":"Costing and measurement decisions","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["**Fencing, edging and wire** depend on the **perimeter**.","**Tiles, paint, roofing and carpet** depend on the **area**."]},{"k":"p","text":"Change all lengths to the same unit before you calculate. Allow for gates, waste, overlaps or several coats of paint if the question says so. Round the number of tiles, tins or packets **up**, because you cannot buy part of one."},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Scaling a shape","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"If every length of a shape is multiplied by $k$, the perimeter is multiplied by $k$ but the area is multiplied by $k^2$. Doubling the sides of a rectangle multiplies its area by $4$."}]},{"k":"box","kind":"tip","title":"Check your answers","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Sketch the shape and label it. Check that perimeters are in m (or cm) and areas in m² (or cm²). Compare the answer with a simple rectangle that is a little larger. If $\\pi$ is not given, use the $\\pi$ key or $3.142$ and say which you used."}]}],"figs":[]}],"examples":[{"title":"Fencing a garden","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A rectangular school garden measures 28 m by 17 m. A 3 m gate is left unfenced. Find (a) the length of wire for one round of fencing, (b) the cost at GH₵42 per metre."}],"steps":["Perimeter: $P=2(28+17)=2\\times45=90$ m.","Leave out the gate: $90-3=87$ m.","Cost: $87\\times42=3654$."],"answer":"(a) 87 m (b) GH₵3,654","figs":[]},{"title":"Tiling a hall","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A hall floor measures 7.5 m by 6.4 m. Square tiles have sides of 40 cm. Ignoring waste, how many tiles are needed?"}],"steps":["Floor area: $7.5\\times6.4=48$ m².","Tile side: $40$ cm $=0.40$ m, so one tile covers $0.40\\times0.40=0.16$ m².","Number of tiles: $48\\div0.16=300$."],"answer":"300 tiles","figs":[]},{"title":"A rectangle with a semicircle","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A courtyard is a 20 m by 12 m rectangle with a semicircle of radius 6 m on one of the 12 m sides. Find the total area in terms of $\\pi$."}],"steps":["Rectangle: $20\\times12=240$ m².","Semicircle: $\\tfrac{1}{2}\\pi r^2=\\tfrac{1}{2}\\pi(6^2)=18\\pi$ m².","The parts do not overlap, so add them."],"answer":"$(240+18\\pi)$ m²","figs":[]},{"title":"A trapezium-shaped plot","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A plot is a trapezium with parallel sides 24 m and 38 m, which are 15 m apart. Find its area and the cost of clearing it at GH₵8.50 per m²."}],"steps":["$A=\\tfrac{1}{2}(a+b)h=\\tfrac{1}{2}(24+38)\\times15=\\tfrac{1}{2}\\times62\\times15=465$ m².","Cost: $465\\times8.50=3952.50$."],"answer":"465 m²; GH₵3,952.50","figs":[]},{"title":"An L-shaped compound","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"An L-shaped compound is a 16 m by 12 m rectangle with a 6 m by 5 m rectangle removed from one corner. Find its area and its perimeter."}],"steps":["Full rectangle: $16\\times12=192$ m². Corner: $6\\times5=30$ m².","Area: $192-30=162$ m².","Removing the corner replaces two edges (6 m and 5 m) with two equal edges (5 m and 6 m) set inwards, so the perimeter does not change: $2(16+12)=56$ m."],"answer":"Area 162 m²; perimeter 56 m.","figs":[]},{"title":"A walkway round a pond","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A circular pond has a diameter of 14 m. A walkway 2 m wide surrounds it. Find the area of the walkway, using $\\pi=\\dfrac{22}{7}$."}],"steps":["Inner radius $=7$ m; outer radius $=7+2=9$ m.","Walkway $=\\pi(9^2-7^2)=\\pi(81-49)=32\\pi$.","$32\\times\\dfrac{22}{7}=\\dfrac{704}{7}\\approx100.57$."],"answer":"About 100.57 m²","figs":[]},{"title":"Painting a board","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A triangular board has a base of 3.2 m and a perpendicular height of 1.75 m. It needs two coats of paint, and 1 litre covers 4 m² in one coat. How many whole litres must be bought?"}],"steps":["Area: $\\tfrac{1}{2}\\times3.2\\times1.75=2.8$ m².","Two coats: $2\\times2.8=5.6$ m².","Paint: $5.6\\div4=1.4$ litres.","Paint is sold in whole litres, so round **up**."],"answer":"2 litres","figs":[]},{"title":"Area in hectares","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A rectangular field is 0.08 km long and 75 m wide. Find its area in hectares and its perimeter in metres."}],"steps":["Same units: $0.08$ km $=80$ m.","Area: $80\\times75=6000$ m² $=6000\\div10\\,000=0.6$ ha.","Perimeter: $2(80+75)=310$ m."],"answer":"0.6 ha; 310 m","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Key results for Week 19","items":["$1$ m² $=10\\,000$ cm²; $\\;1$ ha $=10\\,000$ m².","Rectangle $A=lb$, $P=2(l+b)$; triangle $A=\\tfrac{1}{2}bh$; parallelogram $A=bh$.","Trapezium $A=\\tfrac{1}{2}(a+b)h$; circle $A=\\pi r^2$, $C=2\\pi r$.","Annulus $A=\\pi(R^2-r^2)$.","Fencing uses perimeter; tiling and painting use area. Round whole items up."]}],"quiz":[{"q":"A room measures 8 m by 5 m. Find its area.","options":["63 cm²","126 cm²","23 cm²","46 cm²"],"correct":0,"explain":"$A=\\tfrac{1}{2}\\times14\\times9=63$ cm²."},{"q":"A circular pond has a radius of 4 m. What is its area?","options":["$8\\pi$ m²","$12\\pi$ m²","$16\\pi$ m²","$32\\pi$ m²"],"correct":2,"explain":"$A=\\pi r^2=\\pi\\times4^2=16\\pi$ m²."},{"q":"A 12 m by 9 m courtyard has a 3 m by 4 m flower bed. Its area is","options":["50 cm²","100 cm²","40 cm²","25 cm²"],"correct":0,"explain":"$A=\\tfrac{1}{2}(8+12)\\times5=50$ cm²."},{"q":"A square has an area of 81 m². Find its perimeter.","options":["18 m","36 m","9 m","162 m"],"correct":1,"explain":"Side $=\\sqrt{81}=9$ m; perimeter $=4\\times9=36$ m."},{"q":"Both the length and the breadth of a rectangle are doubled. What happens to the area?","options":["It does not change.","It doubles.","It is multiplied by 4.","It halves."],"correct":2,"explain":"$(2l)(2b)=4lb$."}],"exercise":[{"q":"A 35 m by 24 m plot has one 4 m gate. Find the length of wire needed for three strands of fencing.","a":"$P=2(35+24)=118$ m; $118-4=114$ m; $3\\times114=342$ m."},{"q":"A ring has an outer radius of 9 cm and an inner radius of 5 cm. Find its area in terms of $\\pi$.","a":"$\\pi(81-25)=56\\pi$ cm²"},{"q":"Write 4.8 hectares in m² and in km².","a":"$48\\,000$ m² $=0.048$ km²"},{"q":"Give two rectangles with area 72 m² but different perimeters. It tells you how much ground can be planted."],"answer":"$P=32$ m (a length); $A=60$ m² (a surface).","model":null},{"q":"A rectangle has a perimeter of 58 m and one side of 12 m. Volume is given in **cubic units** such as cm³ or m³."},{"k":"p","text":"To find the volume of a cuboid made of unit cubes, count the cubes in one layer and multiply by the number of layers."},{"k":"fig","id":"w20-cubes","caption":"One layer has $4\\times3=12$ cubes; two layers give $24$ cubes, so $V=4\\times3\\times2=24$ cubic units."},{"k":"p","text":"**Capacity** is the amount a container can hold. It is usually measured in litres (L) or millilitres (mL)."}],"figs":["w20-cubes"]},{"title":"Prisms and cross-sections","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A **prism** is a solid with two identical, parallel end faces and the **same cross-section** all along its length. Cuboids and triangular prisms are prisms. A cylinder has a circular cross-section and is treated in the same way."},{"k":"fig","id":"w20-prism","caption":"Every slice of the prism has the same area $A$, so the volume is the area of one slice times the length."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Volume of a prism","blocks":[{"k":"math","tex":"V=A\\times L"},{"k":"p","text":"$A$ is the area of the cross-section and $L$ is the length of the prism (the distance between the end faces)."}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w20-sections","caption":"The shaded face is the constant cross-section. Do not mix them up."}]}],"figs":["w20-prism","w20-sections"]},{"title":"Units of volume and capacity","blocks":[{"k":"fig","id":"w20-litre","caption":"A cube of side 10 cm holds exactly 1 litre."},{"k":"table","head":["Volume","Capacity"],"rows":[["$1$ cm³","$1$ mL"],["$1000$ cm³","$1$ litre"],["$1$ m³ $=1\\,000\\,000$ cm³","$1000$ litres"]]},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Cube the conversion factor for volume","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Since $1$ m $=100$ cm, $1$ m³ $=100\\times100\\times100=1\\,000\\,000$ cm³. If a container is only partly full, use the depth of the liquid, or multiply the full capacity by the fraction that is filled. Find the side of the cube and give three whole-number measurements for the cuboid.","a":"Cube side 6 cm; for example $12\\times6\\times3$ or $9\\times8\\times3$ cm."},{"q":"Find the volume of a cylinder with radius 7 cm and height 10 cm, using $\\pi=\\dfrac{22}{7}$. Give the answer in litres too.","a":"$\\dfrac{22}{7}\\times49\\times10=1540$ cm³ $=1.54$ litres."},{"q":"Write 3.5 m³ in cm³.","a":"$3.5\\times1\\,000\\,000=3\\,500\\,000$ cm³"},{"q":"Find the total surface area of a cube of side 5 cm.","a":"$6\\times5^2=150$ cm²"}],"theory":[{"q":"Explain why the volume of a prism is its cross-sectional area times its length.","steps":["A prism is made of identical slices, each with the same area $A$.","Like layers of unit cubes, the slices are stacked along the whole length $L$.","So the total space is $A\\times L$ cubic units."],"answer":"$V=A\\times L$, just as volume = (cubes in one layer) × (number of layers).","model":null},{"q":"A tank measures 1.8 m by 1.4 m by 0.9 m inside. The top 20 cm is empty. How many litres of water does it contain?","steps":["Depth of water: $0.9-0.2=0.7$ m.","$V=1.8\\times1.4\\times0.7=1.764$ m³.","$1.764\\times1000=1764$ litres."],"answer":"1764 litres","model":null},{"q":"A triangular prism has a triangle of base 12 cm and height 5 cm, and the prism is 30 cm long. Find its volume.","steps":["$A=\\tfrac{1}{2}\\times12\\times5=30$ cm².","$V=30\\times30=900$ cm³."],"answer":"900 cm³","model":null},{"q":"A solid is a 10 cm by 6 cm by 4 cm cuboid with a rectangular tunnel 3 cm by 2 cm running through its 4 cm thickness. Find its volume.","steps":["Cuboid: $10\\times6\\times4=240$ cm³.","Tunnel: $3\\times2\\times4=24$ cm³.","Solid: $240-24=216$ cm³."],"answer":"216 cm³","model":null},{"q":"Explain why a 2 m³ tank cannot hold 20 000 litres.","steps":["$1$ m³ $=1000$ litres, so $2$ m³ $=2000$ litres.","20 000 litres would need 20 m³.","The mistake is using a factor of 10 000 instead of 1000."],"answer":"The tank holds only 2000 litres.","model":null}],"checklist":["I can explain volume as the number of unit cubes in a solid.","I can identify the cross-section of a prism and use $V=A\\times L$.","I can find volumes of cuboids, triangular prisms and cylinders.","I can convert between cm³, m³ and litres.","I can find the volume of composite solids and solve capacity problems.","I can tell surface area from volume."],"plan":{"lessons":[[{"j":0,"notes":true,"exs":[0]},{"j":1,"notes":true,"exs":[1,2,3]}],[{"j":2,"notes":true,"exs":[4,5]},{"j":3,"notes":true,"exs":[]},{"j":4,"notes":true,"exs":[6,7]}]],"exSec":[0,1,1,1,2,2,4,4],"quizSec":[0,1,0,2,4,1,4,0,1,1],"exerSec":[2,1,1,4,2,1,0,4],"thSec":[1,2,1,3,4],"sumSec":[1,1,2,3,4],"chkSec":[0,1,1,1,3,4],"weights":[1301.95,3669.5,2602.45,260.25,2170.8],"figs":[{"id":"w20-cubes","sec":0,"lesson":1,"caption":"One layer has $4\\times3=12$ cubes; two layers give $24$ cubes, so $V=4\\times3\\times2=24$ cubic units."},{"id":"w20-litre","sec":2,"lesson":2,"caption":"A cube of side 10 cm holds exactly 1 litre."}]},"next":"Understanding Data and Methods of Data Collection","tm":{"sectionNo":7,"sectionName":"Perimeter, Area and Volume","strand":"Geometry Around Us","sub":"Measurement","cs":["Demonstrate conceptual understanding of the measurement of perimeter and area of 2-D shapes and quadrilaterals.","Demonstrate conceptual understanding of the measurement of surface area, volume and capacity of solid shapes."],"lo":["Identify and compare referents for SI and imperial area measurements, estimate the perimeter and area of 2-D shapes and solve related problems.","Determine the volume and capacity of solid shapes and solve problems that involve SI and imperial units."],"indicators":["Solve problems that involve SI and imperial units in volume of prisms.","Solve real world problems that involve the volume of prisms."],"focal":[],"exemplars":[],"flags":[],"source":"tm","assess":[]},"figImgs":{"w20-cubes":{"png":"","w":380.0,"h":210.0,"pw":760,"ph":420,"doc":"","dw":380,"dh":251.75},"w20-litre":{"png":"","w":380.0,"h":170.0,"pw":760,"ph":340,"doc":"","dw":380,"dh":194.875}}}</script>
<script type="application/json" id="pack-y1w21">{"year":1,"week":21,"id":"y1w21","title":"Understanding Data and Methods of Data Collection","subtitle":"Data and statistics; population and sample; quantitative (discrete and continuous) and qualitative (nominal and ordinal) data; primary and secondary data; questionnaires, interviews, observation and records; fair sampling and ethics.","family":"data","section":{"no":4,"name":"Data and Probability","strand":"Making Sense of and Using Data","from":21,"to":24},"outcomes":["Explain what data and statistics are, and write a clear statistical question.","Distinguish a population from a sample, and a census from a sample survey.","Classify data as discrete, continuous, nominal or ordinal, and as primary or secondary.","Choose and justify a suitable method of collecting data, and write neutral survey questions.","Select a fair sample, including a proportionate stratified sample, and handle data ethically."],"keywords":["data","statistics","variable","population","sample","census","quantitative","qualitative","discrete","continuous","nominal","ordinal","primary data","secondary data","questionnaire","bias","stratified sample"],"notes":[{"title":"Data and statistics","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"**Data** are facts, counts, measurements or descriptions collected to answer a question. **Statistics** is the work of collecting, organising, analysing and interpreting data."},{"k":"p","text":"Good work starts with a **clear question**. “How long do Year 1 learners take to travel to school?” is clear; “What about travel?” is not. Decide exactly which **variable** you will record and how you will measure it."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Population, sample and variable","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Key terms","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["The **population** is the whole group you want to find out about, for example all 1,200 learners in a school.","A **sample** is a smaller group chosen from the population.","A **census** collects data from every member of the population.","A **variable** is a characteristic that can differ from person to person (height, transport, age); each recorded value is an **observation**."]}]},{"k":"p","text":"How the sample is chosen matters as much as its size. Asking only the first 20 learners at the gate may leave out learners who travel far or arrive late."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Types of data","blocks":[{"k":"fig","id":"w21-types","caption":"Quantitative data are numbers (counted or measured); qualitative data are categories (unordered or ranked)."},{"k":"table","head":["Type","Meaning","Examples"],"rows":[["Discrete","counted; usually whole numbers","number of siblings, books, absentees"],["Continuous","measured; any value in a range","height, mass, time, temperature"],["Nominal","categories with no order","favourite subject, transport, colour"],["Ordinal","categories with a natural order","poor/fair/good, 1st/2nd/3rd"]]},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Numbers that are not quantities","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A phone number or a learner’s ID number is made of digits, but it is a **label**, not a quantity: it makes no sense to find its average. Coding categories as 1 = bus and 2 = bicycle does not turn transport into quantitative data."}]}],"figs":["w21-types"]},{"title":"Primary and secondary data","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["**Primary data** are collected by you for your own study: surveys, interviews, observations or experiments.","**Secondary data** already exist: school registers, census reports, newspapers or websites."]},{"k":"p","text":"Before using secondary data, check the **source**, the **date**, the **definitions** used and whether the data are **complete**."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Methods of collecting data","blocks":[{"k":"fig","id":"w21-methods","caption":"Four common ways to collect data."},{"k":"ul","items":["**Questionnaire:** many people answer the same written questions. Multiple-choice items are quick to count; open questions give reasons.","**Interview:** questions asked face to face. You can follow up answers, but it takes time and the interviewer can influence replies.","**Observation:** watch and record events with a checklist or tally, for example vehicles passing a gate.","**Existing records:** registers, receipts or reports (secondary data), used with permission."]},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Avoid leading questions","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"“Don’t you agree the canteen is too expensive?” pushes people towards one answer. Ask instead: “How would you rate the canteen prices: very low, low, fair, high, very high?” Try your questions on a few people first (a **pilot**) to find unclear wording."}]}],"figs":["w21-methods"]},{"title":"Sampling fairly","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["**Simple random sample:** every member has the same chance of being chosen, for example names drawn from the register.","**Stratified sample:** the population is split into groups (strata) and each group is sampled in proportion to its size.","**Convenience sample:** whoever is easiest to reach. It is quick but often **biased**."]},{"k":"fig","id":"w21-sampling","caption":"A random sample (left) and a stratified sample (right) that keeps the proportions of girls and boys."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Proportionate stratified sample","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Number to choose from a group:"},{"k":"math","tex":"\\frac{\\text{group size}}{\\text{population size}}\\times\\text{sample size}"}]},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Ethics","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Take part only with consent; do not collect names or private information unless they are really needed; keep answers confidential; and report results honestly."}]}],"figs":["w21-sampling"]},{"title":"Data quality","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Before analysing, check that all values use the **same units**, that no answers are missing, and that categories do not overlap (for example “0–5 km” and “5–10 km” overlap at 5). Good graphs cannot repair badly collected data. In Week 22 we organise data into tables and graphs."}],"figs":[]}],"examples":[{"title":"Classifying variables","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A class survey records each learner’s height, age in completed years, favourite subject and satisfaction (low, medium, high). Classify each variable."}],"steps":["Height is measured and can take decimal values: quantitative, **continuous**.","Age in completed years is a whole number: quantitative, **discrete**.","Favourite subject has no order: qualitative, **nominal**.","Satisfaction has an order (low $<$ medium $<$ high): qualitative, **ordinal**."],"answer":"Continuous; discrete; nominal; ordinal.","figs":[]},{"title":"Is the sample fair?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A researcher wants the average travel time of all 900 learners in a school. She asks the first 30 learners who arrive. Name the population and the sample, and comment on the method."}],"steps":["Population: all 900 learners. Sample: the 30 early arrivals.","This is a convenience sample.","Early arrivals may live closer or use faster transport, so the result may be biased.","Better: choose learners at random from the school register, or stratify by community."],"answer":"Population 900, sample 30; the convenience sample is likely to be biased.","figs":[]},{"title":"Codes are not quantities","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A school records shoe sizes using the codes 1, 2, 3 and 4 for four size groups. Is it sensible to find the mean of the codes?"}],"steps":["The codes stand for ordered size groups, not amounts.","The gaps between the groups may not be equal, so arithmetic on the codes has no clear meaning.","To calculate an average, record the actual shoe sizes instead."],"answer":"No. The codes are ordinal labels; record real sizes if you need a mean.","figs":[]},{"title":"Watching a queue","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"To study lunch queues, a learner counts how many people join the canteen line in each 5-minute interval for one hour. Name the method and the type of data, and give one limitation."}],"steps":["Method: direct, structured observation.","The counts are quantitative, discrete data; there are $60\\div5=12$ intervals.","One hour on one day may not represent other days.","Improvement: repeat on several days at the same times."],"answer":"Observation; discrete data; one day may not be typical.","figs":[]},{"title":"A stratified sample","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A school has 600 learners: 360 girls and 240 boys. Choose a proportionate stratified sample of 50."}],"steps":["Girls: $\\dfrac{360}{600}\\times50=0.6\\times50=30$.","Boys: $\\dfrac{240}{600}\\times50=0.4\\times50=20$.","Check: $30+20=50$ ✓. Choose randomly within each group."],"answer":"30 girls and 20 boys","figs":[]},{"title":"Fixing a biased question","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A questionnaire asks: “Since online lessons are better than classroom lessons, which do you prefer?” Explain the problem and rewrite the question."}],"steps":["The first part states an opinion as a fact, which leads people to one answer.","Neutral version: “Which kind of lesson do you prefer: online, classroom, a mixture, or no preference?”","Add an optional question asking for reasons."],"answer":"Remove the leading statement and give balanced choices.","figs":[]},{"title":"Secondary records","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A canteen manager uses last year’s payment records to estimate spending this year. What kind of data is this, and what two checks should be made?"}],"steps":["The records already exist, so they are **secondary** data.","Check that prices and buying habits have not changed much since last year.","Check that the records are complete (for example, no missing cash payments)."],"answer":"Secondary data; check that they are up to date and complete.","figs":[]},{"title":"Mixed units","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A learner records 12 classroom temperatures, some in °C and some in °F. How should the data be cleaned?"}],"steps":["Find the unit of every reading.","Convert the °F readings using $C=(F-32)\\times\\dfrac{5}{9}$; for example $86^\\circ\\text{F}=(86-32)\\times\\dfrac{5}{9}=30^\\circ\\text{C}$.","Record all values in °C (keeping the original readings), and only then calculate averages."],"answer":"Convert every reading to the same unit before any analysis.","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Key results for Week 21","items":["Population: the whole group. Sample: part of it. Census: every member.","Quantitative: discrete (counted) or continuous (measured). Qualitative: nominal (no order) or ordinal (ordered).","Primary data: collected by you. Secondary data: already existing.","Stratified sample: $\\dfrac{\\text{group size}}{\\text{population}}\\times\\text{sample size}$.","Use neutral questions, random selection, consent and consistent units."]}],"quiz":[{"q":"A learner’s mass of 52.4 kg is an example of","options":["discrete quantitative data","continuous quantitative data","nominal data","ordinal data"],"correct":1,"explain":"Mass is measured and can take decimal values."},{"q":"The number of learners absent on Monday is","options":["discrete quantitative data","continuous data","nominal data","ordinal data"],"correct":0,"explain":"Absentees are counted in whole numbers."},{"q":"Which variable is nominal?","options":["position in a test","temperature","preferred way of travelling to school","height"],"correct":2,"explain":"Ways of travelling are categories with no natural order."},{"q":"The ratings excellent, good, fair, poor are","options":["nominal","continuous","discrete","ordinal"],"correct":3,"explain":"The categories have a meaningful order."},{"q":"New answers collected directly from learners for your study are","options":["secondary data","primary data","always a census","published data"],"correct":1,"explain":"Data you collect yourself for your own study are primary data."},{"q":"In a study of all 450 Year 1 learners, what is the population?","options":["the 30 learners surveyed","their teachers","all 450 Year 1 learners","the school building"],"correct":2,"explain":"The population is the whole group the study is about."},{"q":"Which question is least likely to lead the person answering?","options":["How would you rate the canteen prices?","Why are canteen prices unfair?","Don’t you think the food is expensive?","Surely you agree prices should drop?"],"correct":0,"explain":"It does not assume what the answer will be."},{"q":"Choosing 20 learners by drawing names at random from a list of 200 is","options":["convenience sampling","snowball sampling","a census","simple random sampling"],"correct":3,"explain":"Every learner on the list has the same chance of being chosen."},{"q":"Which method is best for counting vehicles passing the school gate?","options":["an unstructured opinion interview","an observation tally","a favourite-subject questionnaire","reading old articles only"],"correct":1,"explain":"Watching and tallying records the vehicles directly."},{"q":"Why must readings in °C and °F be changed to one unit?","options":["to increase the sample size","to remove all bias","so that all measurements use the same scale","to change continuous data into nominal data"],"correct":2,"explain":"Averages and comparisons need consistent units."}],"exercise":[{"q":"Write a five-question survey on how learners travel to school and how long it takes. (continuous) (3) How many times were you late last week? (discrete) (4) How safe is your journey: very safe / safe / unsafe? (ordinal) (5) Which community do you live in? (nominal)"},{"q":"A school has 480 boarders and 320 day learners. Find the numbers of each in a proportionate sample of 80.","a":"Total 800: boarders $\\dfrac{480}{800}\\times80=48$; day learners $\\dfrac{320}{800}\\times80=32$."},{"q":"Describe how you would observe how often litter is dropped in the school compound without identifying anyone.","a":"Choose fixed places and times; use a tally sheet to count litter items or littering events in each interval; record no names or photographs of faces; repeat on several days."},{"q":"Classify: phone number, number of textbooks, height, house colour, examination position.","a":"Phone number: a label (nominal, not a quantity); textbooks: discrete; height: continuous; house colour: nominal; examination position: ordinal."},{"q":"Rewrite this item in neutral words: “Don’t you agree that the library is too small?”","a":"“How would you describe the size of the library: too small, about right, or too large?”"},{"q":"Is each primary or secondary data? (a) a Ghana Statistical Service census report (b) heights you measure in your class.","a":"(a) secondary (b) primary"},{"q":"Give one advantage of a sample over a census, and one advantage of a census over a sample.","a":"A sample is quicker and cheaper; a census includes everyone, so it is not affected by sampling error."},{"q":"Convert $77^\\circ$F to °C.","a":"$(77-32)\\times\\dfrac{5}{9}=45\\times\\dfrac{5}{9}=25^\\circ$C"}],"theory":[{"q":"Use school examples to explain continuous, discrete, nominal and ordinal data.","steps":["Continuous: measured values such as height (1.62 m) or travel time; decimals are possible.","Discrete: counts such as the number of textbooks.","Nominal: unordered categories such as house colour or favourite subject.","Ordinal: ordered categories such as examination position or a satisfaction rating."],"answer":"Measured, counted, unordered categories, ordered categories.","model":null},{"q":"A school has 720 learners in Year 1 and 480 in Year 2. Secondary: convenient but possibly unsuitable.","model":null},{"q":"Suggest a fair way to compare the travel times of learners from two communities.","steps":["Define the variable: minutes from leaving home to arriving at school.","Take a random (or stratified) sample of consenting learners from each community.","Use the same questions, on similar days, and keep identities private."],"answer":"One clear variable, random samples from both communities, the same method for everyone.","model":null},{"q":"A questionnaire asks learners whether they agree that “the school library is excellent”. Criticise the question and improve it.","steps":["The word “excellent” suggests the answer, so it may bias the results.","Better: “How would you rate the school library?” with balanced options: very poor, poor, fair, good, very good, and “I have not used it”."],"answer":"Use a neutral question with balanced answer choices.","model":null}],"checklist":["I can explain population, sample, census and variable.","I can classify data as discrete, continuous, nominal or ordinal.","I can tell primary from secondary data.","I can choose a suitable method of collecting data and write neutral questions.","I can work out a proportionate stratified sample.","I can check data quality and collect data ethically."],"plan":{"lessons":[[{"j":0,"notes":true,"exs":[]},{"j":1,"notes":true,"exs":[0,1]},{"j":2,"notes":true,"exs":[2]},{"j":3,"notes":true,"exs":[]}],[{"j":4,"notes":true,"exs":[3]},{"j":5,"notes":true,"exs":[4,5]},{"j":6,"notes":true,"exs":[6,7]}]],"exSec":[1,1,2,4,5,5,6,6],"quizSec":[2,2,2,2,3,1,4,5,4,1],"exerSec":[2,1,4,2,4,3,5,0],"thSec":[2,1,3,4,4],"sumSec":[1,2,3,1,5],"chkSec":[1,2,3,4,5,6],"weights":[336.15,2016.45,1734,300.4,1628.45,2501.5,1672.9],"figs":[{"id":"w21-types","sec":2,"lesson":1,"caption":"Quantitative data are numbers (counted or measured); <script type="application/json" id="pack-y1w22">{"year":1,"week":22,"id":"y1w22","title":"Organising and Presenting Data; Mean, Median and Mode","subtitle":"Frequency tables and grouped data; bar charts, pie charts, histograms and line graphs; the mean, median and mode; the range and the effect of outliers; using a spreadsheet.","family":"data","section":{"no":4,"name":"Data and Probability","strand":"Making Sense of and Using Data","from":21,"to":24},"outcomes":["Organise raw data into ungrouped and grouped frequency tables.","Draw and read bar charts, pie charts, histograms and line graphs, and spot misleading graphs.","Calculate the mean, median, mode and range, including from frequency tables.","Estimate the mean of grouped data using class midpoints.","Choose the most suitable average and explain the effect of outliers."],"keywords":["raw data","frequency table","relative frequency","class interval","midpoint","bar chart","pie chart","histogram","line graph","mean","median","mode","range","outlier"],"notes":[{"title":"From raw data to a frequency table","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"**Raw data** are the observations as they were collected. Twelve learners give the number of books they read in a month:"},{"k":"math","tex":"1,\\ 3,\\ 2,\\ 1,\\ 4,\\ 2,\\ 3,\\ 2,\\ 1,\\ 5,\\ 2,\\ 4"},{"k":"p","text":"It is hard to see the pattern. A **frequency table** groups equal values and counts them (tally marks in groups of five make counting easy):"},{"k":"table","head":["Books read, $x$","1","2","3","4","5","Total"],"rows":[["Frequency, $f$","3","4","2","2","1","12"]]},{"k":"box","kind":"tip","title":"Always check the total","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The frequencies must add up to the number of observations: $3+4+2+2+1=12$ ✓."}]},{"k":"p","text":"The **relative frequency** of a value is $\\dfrac{\\text{frequency}}{\\text{total}}$; multiply by $100\\%$ to get a percentage. For example, 2 books has relative frequency $\\dfrac{4}{12}=\\dfrac{1}{3}\\approx33\\%$."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Grouped data","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"When there are many different values, group them into **class intervals** such as $0$–$9$, $10$–$19$, $20$–$29$. The classes must not overlap, and every value must fit in exactly one class."},{"k":"ul","items":["The **class width** of $10$–$19$ is $10$.","The **midpoint** is the average of the class limits: $\\dfrac{10+19}{2}=14.5$."]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Presenting data","blocks":[{"k":"fig","id":"w22-bar","caption":"A bar chart compares categories or separate values. The bars have gaps and start from zero."},{"k":"fig","id":"w22-pie","caption":"A pie chart shows how a whole is shared. Each member of the club is worth $9^\\circ$."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Pie chart angles","blocks":[{"k":"math","tex":"\\text{sector angle}=\\frac{\\text{frequency}}{\\text{total frequency}}\\times360^\\circ"},{"k":"p","text":"The angles must add up to $360^\\circ$."}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w22-histogram","caption":"A histogram shows grouped numerical data. The bars touch because the classes follow on from each other."},{"k":"fig","id":"w22-line","caption":"A line graph shows how a quantity changes over time."},{"k":"table","head":["Graph","Best used for"],"rows":[["Bar chart","comparing categories (bars with gaps)"],["Pie chart","parts of a whole"],["Histogram","grouped numerical data (bars touching)"],["Line graph","change over time"]]},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Honest graphs","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Give every graph a title, labelled axes with units, an even scale and a key if needed. A bar chart’s axis should start at **zero**; otherwise the bars’ lengths mislead. Avoid 3-D effects that distort the sizes."}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w22-axis","caption":"The same club sizes drawn two ways. Starting the axis at 10 hides clubs B and D and exaggerates the differences."}],"figs":["w22-bar","w22-pie","w22-histogram","w22-line","w22-axis"]},{"title":"The three averages","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Mean, median and mode","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["**Mean:** $\\bar{x}=\\dfrac{\\text{sum of the values}}{\\text{number of values}}=\\dfrac{\\sum x}{n}$","**Mean from a frequency table:** $\\bar{x}=\\dfrac{\\sum fx}{\\sum f}$","**Median:** the middle value when the data are in order. For $n$ values it is the $\\left(\\dfrac{n+1}{2}\\right)$th value; if $n$ is even, it is the mean of the two middle values.","**Mode:** the value that occurs most often. There may be one mode, more than one, or none."]}]},{"k":"p","text":"For grouped data, use the class **midpoints** as $x$ in $\\dfrac{\\sum fx}{\\sum f}$. The answer is an **estimate**, because we do not know the exact values inside each class."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Range, outliers and choosing an average","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The **range** is the largest value minus the smallest value. It measures the spread but depends only on the two extremes."},{"k":"p","text":"An **outlier** is a value far from the rest. It pulls the mean towards it but hardly moves the median."},{"k":"fig","id":"w22-outlier","caption":"Eight fares are between GH₵5 and GH₵9, but one is GH₵44. The median (7) describes a typical fare better than the mean (11.11)."},{"k":"table","head":["Average","Strength","Use it when…"],"rows":[["Mean","uses every value","the data have no extreme values"],["Median","not affected by outliers","there are extreme values, e.g. incomes or fares"],["Mode","works for categories too","you want the most popular item, e.g. a shoe size"]]}],"figs":["w22-outlier"]},{"title":"Using a spreadsheet","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"In a spreadsheet, `SUM` adds values, `AVERAGE` gives the mean, `MEDIAN` gives the median, `MODE.SNGL` gives a single mode and `COUNT` counts the numbers. The conclusions often lead to a new, sharper question."},{"k":"p","text":"The plan states the **population**, a manageable **sample**, the **method** of collecting data, how the data will be organised, and what will be compared."}],"figs":["w23-cycle"]},{"title":"Populations, samples and bias","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The **population** is the whole group the conclusion is about; the **sample** is the members actually studied. The six outcomes are **equally likely** only if the die is fair."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Probability and the probability scale","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Probability of an event","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"For equally likely outcomes:"},{"k":"math","tex":"P(E)=\\frac{\\text{number of outcomes in }E}{\\text{total number of outcomes}}"}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w24-scale","caption":"Every probability lies between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain)."},{"k":"ul","items":["$0\\leq P(E)\\leq1$; an impossible event has probability $0$ and a certain event has probability $1$.","The **complement** $E'$ means “$E$ does not happen”: $\\;P(E')=1-P(E)$.","Probabilities can be written as fractions, decimals or percentages: $\\dfrac{1}{8}=0.125=12.5\\%$."]},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Only for equally likely outcomes","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The formula $\\dfrac{\\text{favourable}}{\\text{total}}$ works only when every outcome is equally likely. With many trials it gets close to the theoretical probability."}],"figs":["w24-scale"]},{"title":"Compound experiments and sample spaces","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A **compound** experiment has two or more stages, such as tossing a coin and then rolling a die.
